reason: The highest-scoring candidate at the head of the chapter, and the pairing is genuinely affecting: Esther pleads “how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?” and Mormon opens “I finish my record concerning the destruction of my people, the Nephites.” But the shared run is four ordinary words and the fifth word diverges — Esther has “kindred”, Mormon has “people” — and the two sentences do opposite work. Esther's is a plea made while the destruction can still be stopped, and it is stopped; Mormon's is a colophon written after it has happened, in the past tense, by the man who watched. Nothing else of Esther 8 is present. Recorded because a reader who notices the phrase should be told the catalogue noticed it too.

The second-highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a real trap, because “fall into the hands of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Hebrews 10:31, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” — and Mormon 6:6 is a fearful sentence about things falling into hands. The senses do not meet at any point. Hebrews is about a person falling under the judgment of God, which is the worst thing that can happen to an apostate; Mormon 6:6 is about sacred records falling under the custody of an enemy who would burn them, which is a logistical fear about objects. A five-word run and pure KJV boilerplate for a civilian population; the catalogue's standing exclusion on connective formulae covers it. The machine matched four connective words, but the reason to write this up is typological, and it is the strongest typological pull in the chapter. Judges 19-21 is the Bible's one narrative of a whole tribe of Israel being hunted to near-extinction by its own brother tribes, ending with a remnant of six hundred men and a national lament — and Mormon 6 is the Book of Mormon's account of a whole branch of the house of Israel being hunted to extinction by its own brother nation, ending with a remnant of twenty-four and a lament. The wording will not carry it. Judges 20:48 shares nothing distinctive with Mormon 6:8; “smote them with the edge of the sword” does not appear in Mormon 6, whose weapons list at 6:9 is its own; and the surviving numbers, six hundred against twenty-four, are not in any relation. Jeremiah's is the prophetic triad of judgments — sword, famine, pestilence — three agencies by which God consumes a nation that will not serve Babylon. Mormon's is an inventory of hardware: sword, bow, arrow, axe, “and with all manner of weapons of war.” Neither famine nor pestilence appears in Mormon 6, and no weapon appears in Jeremiah 27:8 but the sword. Note also that “weapons of war” is not available as evidence here: it occurs 44 times in the Book of Mormon, overwhelmingly in Alma, and is this book's own standing phrase. reason: Not proposed by any machine stream, and written up because it is the parallel a reader is most likely to arrive at unaided. Josiah is the last good king of Judah; he goes out to a battle he is warned against, is shot by archers, is carried wounded from the field, and dies — after which Jeremiah composes a lament for him and the lamentations become an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:20-25). Mormon is the last righteous commander of the Nephites; he goes out to a battle he knows is the last, is wounded and left for dead among his ten thousand, survives, and composes the lament. The correspondence extends to the lamenting prophet being Jeremiah, whose 9:1 does stand behind Mormon 6:16. But there is no verbal contact: 2 Chronicles 35:23 reads “the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded”, and Mormon 6:10 reads “I fell wounded in the midst; and they passed by me that they did not put an end to my life”. The only shared word is “wounded”. “Wounded in the midst” occurs in no KJV verse. The Megiddo–Cumorah reading is worth a reader's time and is not dependence; where the wording does bear, at “fallen … in the midst”, the source is 2 Samuel 1:25 and the link is at 6:13.
